body:
From opposition to British policies to Indian nationalism

Indian nationalism developed gradually during the 19th century. As British rule expanded and colonial policies affected different sections of Indian society, educated Indians increasingly questioned how the country was governed and whose interests the government served.

The Revolt of 1857 had challenged British authority, but it had not produced a permanent, nationwide political organisation with a common programme. In the following decades, a different form of political activity emerged. Lawyers, teachers, journalists, merchants and other educated Indians established associations, organised meetings and submitted demands to the colonial government.

These activities contributed to the growth of modern political nationalism: the belief that Indians, despite their differences in religion, caste, language and region, possessed common political interests and should have a voice in governing their country.

Political nationalism

Political nationalism is the belief that people who identify with a common nation should be able to participate in decisions concerning its government, resources and collective future. In colonial India, this belief gradually developed into the demand for Indian self-government.

Why did political nationalism grow?

Economic dissatisfaction

British economic policies were increasingly criticised for benefiting British interests while contributing to poverty and economic difficulties in India. Heavy land-revenue demands burdened cultivators, traditional industries faced difficulties, and important government expenditure served colonial interests.

Educated Indians began investigating these problems through economic statistics, government reports and public debate. They increasingly connected economic hardship with the political system under which economic decisions were made.

Racial discrimination and exclusion from administration

Although Indians could obtain modern education and professional qualifications, important administrative positions remained dominated by Europeans. Indian political leaders argued that qualified Indians should have greater opportunities in the civil services and government institutions.

The inequality was not merely a question of employment. It also raised a political issue: if Indians were considered capable of obtaining education and performing professional duties, why should they be denied equal opportunities to exercise authority?

Western education and new means of communication

Modern education introduced many Indians to ideas such as liberty, equality, representative government and constitutional rights. English also became a language through which educated people from different linguistic regions could communicate.

Newspapers, printing presses, railways and postal networks helped political arguments circulate beyond individual towns. Indian political leaders could communicate grievances to audiences in different provinces and coordinate public activities.

These developments did not immediately create mass nationalism. Political activity remained concentrated among relatively small educated groups, but the foundations of wider national cooperation were being established.

Government policies that intensified political dissatisfaction

The Arms Act and Vernacular Press Act, 1878

During the viceroyalty of Lord Lytton, the colonial government enacted the Arms Act and Vernacular Press Act in 1878.

  • Arms Act, 1878: Imposed restrictions on the possession of arms, including discriminatory licensing provisions that disadvantaged Indians.
  • Vernacular Press Act, 1878: Restricted newspapers published in Indian languages and gave the government powers to act against publications considered objectionable.

The press law particularly angered educated Indians because newspapers had become important instruments for criticising government policies and communicating public grievances. The Vernacular Press Act was subsequently repealed in 1882 under Lord Ripon.

The Ilbert Bill controversy, 1883

Another major controversy arose during the viceroyalty of Lord Ripon. The Ilbert Bill, introduced in 1883, sought to remove racial restrictions that prevented qualified Indian judges from trying European British subjects in certain criminal cases.

Many Europeans in India strongly opposed the proposal. Their objections revealed an unwillingness to accept Indian judges as equals, even when those judges held the required qualifications and official positions.

The original proposal was substantially diluted through a compromise enacted in 1884. The revised arrangement retained special protections for European defendants, including the right to claim trial by a jury with at least half its members European or American.

For Indian political leaders, the controversy demonstrated that appeals to British principles of equality did not necessarily produce equal treatment under colonial rule. It also strengthened the argument for coordinated political action by Indians across provinces.

The Ilbert Bill distinction

The Ilbert Bill controversy concerned racial equality in judicial authority. It was not a proposal to establish an Indian parliament or grant independence. The original equality proposal was weakened; it was not implemented in its original form.

Why an all-India organisation became necessary

By the early 1880s, political associations were operating in important centres such as Calcutta, Bombay, Poona and Madras. Although these associations raised similar demands, their activities were often organised separately.

A national political organisation could bring representatives from different provinces together, identify common grievances and present a more coordinated programme to the government.

This growing demand for cooperation, together with the experience gained through regional associations and political campaigns, prepared the ground for the establishment of the Indian National Congress in 1885.

Prelims focus

  • The growth of political nationalism accelerated through regional associations during the 1870s and 1880s.
  • The Arms Act and Vernacular Press Act were enacted in 1878 under Lord Lytton.
  • Lord Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882.
  • The Ilbert Bill controversy occurred in 1883 under Lord Ripon.
  • The Indian National Congress was established in 1885.
  • Trap: The Ilbert Bill dealt with the jurisdiction of Indian judges over European defendants, not the establishment of representative legislatures.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 109–111, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Nationalism in India, opening section; Law and History Review, Constitutional Panic in British India: How the Ilbert Bill Controversy of 1883 Revealed the Constitutive Character of Racial Discrimination in the British Empire, discussion of the 1884 compromise, consulted 20 November 2026; Cambridge University Press, Modern Asian Studies, The Indian Press 1870–1880: A Small World of Journalism, discussion of the Vernacular Press Act, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: The Rise of Political Nationalism in British India

body:
The importance of early political associations

The Indian National Congress did not emerge suddenly in 1885. Several political associations had already developed methods of organised public activity during the preceding decades.

These associations brought people together to discuss government policies, prepare petitions, demand reforms and communicate grievances to British authorities. They helped establish the practice of organised political representation.

However, the earliest associations differed considerably in their membership and objectives. Some mainly protected the interests of landlords, while later organisations increasingly represented educated professionals and claimed to speak for wider sections of Indian society.

Important pre-Congress political associations

AssociationYearCentreImportant association
Landholders' Society1838CalcuttaDwarkanath Tagore; protection of landholders' interests
Bengal British India Society1843CalcuttaAssociated with George Thompson; wider discussion of Indian public affairs
British Indian Association1851CalcuttaRadhakanta Deb and Debendranath Tagore; constitutional petitions
Bombay Association1852BombayJagannath Shankarsheth and other Bombay public figures
Madras Native Association1852MadrasGazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty; public grievances and petitions
East India Association1866LondonDadabhai Naoroji; explaining Indian concerns to British audiences
Poona Sarvajanik Sabha1870PoonaG. V. Joshi and M. G. Ranade; organised public representation
Indian League1875CalcuttaSisir Kumar Ghosh; political education and nationalist awareness
Indian Association1876CalcuttaSurendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose
Madras Mahajana Sabha1884MadrasM. Viraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Ananda Charlu
Gujarat Sabha1884AhmedabadLocal professionals; representation of public grievances
Bombay Presidency Association1885BombayPherozeshah Mehta, Badruddin Tyabji and K. T. Telang

How the associations developed

Early associations represented particular social interests

The Landholders' Society, commonly dated to 1838, mainly represented the interests of landlords in the Bengal Presidency. It adopted organised petitions and representations to seek changes in government policies.

The Bengal British India Society, established in 1843, was associated with efforts to discuss Indian affairs and communicate information about conditions in British India.

In 1851, these 2 associations combined to form the British Indian Association. The new organisation continued constitutional petitioning and sought changes in colonial administration and legislation.

The East India Association took Indian concerns to Britain

Dadabhai Naoroji established the East India Association in London in 1866. It aimed to influence British public opinion and communicate Indian grievances to people who could affect decisions about colonial government.

This was important because major decisions affecting India could be made in Britain. Indian political leaders therefore believed that informing British politicians and the public might help secure reforms.

The East India Association was established in London in 1866, whereas the Indian Association was established in Calcutta in 1876. They were different organisations.

The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha developed organised public representation

The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha was established in 1870. Ganesh Vasudeo Joshi, popularly known as Sarvajanik Kaka, and Mahadev Govind Ranade were important figures associated with its activities.

The expression sarvajanik refers to something concerning the public or the people generally. The organisation sought to communicate public grievances to the government and became influential in political discussion in western India.

Its activities included petitions and representations on administrative and economic matters. It helped develop the idea that government decisions should take public opinion into account.

The Indian Association sought broader political cooperation

Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose established the Indian Association in Calcutta in 1876.

It sought to bring educated Indians into political activity and to coordinate opposition to policies considered harmful to Indian interests. Its campaigns included demands concerning the Indian Civil Service examination and opposition to restrictions on the press.

Compared with earlier landlord-dominated associations, the Indian Association placed greater emphasis on broader political participation and cooperation across regions.

The Indian National Conference of 1883

The Indian Association organised an Indian National Conference in Calcutta in December 1883.

The conference brought together representatives concerned with political and administrative reform. Its discussions included representative councils, education, opportunities for Indians in government employment and the separation of judicial and executive functions.

A second National Conference was held in Calcutta in December 1885, around the same time that the first Congress session took place in Bombay.

These conferences demonstrated that Indian political leaders were already attempting to organise cooperation beyond individual provinces before the Congress was established.

National Conference and National Congress

The Indian National Conference of 1883 was organised through the Indian Association. It was an important precursor to the Indian National Congress, but it was not the first session of the Congress. The Congress began separately in Bombay in December 1885.

The Gujarat connection: Gujarat Sabha, Ahmedabad

The Gujarat Sabha was established in Ahmedabad in 1884 as a political body intended to represent public grievances before the government.

It developed within the political environment of the Bombay Presidency, which included much of present-day Gujarat. Educated professionals and local public figures used the organisation to communicate public concerns.

The Gujarat Sabha initially followed a comparatively moderate political approach. It later became associated with important nationalist activities, but its establishment in 1884 belongs to the period before the formation of the Congress.

The Gujarat Sabha should not be confused with the Gujarat Vernacular Society, which was primarily associated with educational, literary and social activities.

How the associations prepared the ground for the Congress

The associations contributed to national political organisation in several ways:

  • They developed experience in conducting meetings, preparing petitions and presenting resolutions.
  • They established connections among lawyers, journalists, teachers and other politically active Indians.
  • They helped political demands circulate across provincial boundaries.
  • They promoted the idea that grievances affecting different regions could be addressed through a common political programme.

Their contribution was therefore not confined to obtaining immediate concessions. They helped create the organisational experience and political awareness needed for an all-India nationalist body.

Prelims focus

  • British Indian Association: Calcutta, 1851.
  • East India Association: Dadabhai Naoroji, London, 1866.
  • Poona Sarvajanik Sabha: 1870; associated with G. V. Joshi and M. G. Ranade.
  • Indian Association: Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose, 1876.
  • Madras Mahajana Sabha: 1884.
  • Gujarat Sabha: Ahmedabad, 1884; Bombay Presidency Association: Bombay, 1885.
  • Trap: The Indian National Conference began in 1883; the Indian National Congress began in 1885.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Emergence of Nationalism, printed pp. 110–111; Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Press Information Bureau, Sir Surendranath Banerjea, section on the Indian Association and National Conference, consulted 20 November 2026; Government of Maharashtra, Maharashtra State Gazetteers, The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870), introductory history; The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Volume 14, printed p. 144, editorial note concerning the Gujarat Sabha, consulted 20 November 2026; Pareeksha, Modern India and the Freedom Struggle, Political Associations, comparative association directory, consulted 20 November 2026.]
